etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English before / bifore, from Old English beforan, from be- + foran (“before”), from fore, from Proto-Germanic *furai, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“front”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian befoar (“before”), German Low German bevör (“before”), German bevor (“before”).

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter V, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: We made an odd party before the arrival of the Ten, particularly when the Celebrity dropped in for lunch or dinner.

quote.citation: 1909, Archibald Marshall [pseudonym; Arthur Hammond Marshall], chapter I, in The Squire’s Daughter, New York, N.Y.: Dodd, Mead and Company, published 1919, →OCLC:
quote.text: He tried to persuade Cicely to stay away from the ball-room for a fourth dance. quote.citation: 2013 September-October, Henry Petroski, “The Evolution of Eyeglasses”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: The ability of a segment of a glass sphere to magnify whatever is placed before it was known around the year 1000, when the spherical segment was called a reading stone, essentially what today we might term a frameless magnifying glass or plain glass paperweight.

quote.citation: 1726, John Ayliffe, Parergon Juris Canonici Anglicani:
quote.text: If a suit be begun before an archdeacon […]

definitions.definition: In store for, in the future of (someone).

quote.text: The golden age […] is before us.

quote.text: There is an Eternity behind thee as well as one before. Hast thou bewailed the aeons that passed without thee, who art so much afraid of the aeons that shall pass?

definitions.definition: In front of, according to a formal system of ordering items.
At a higher or greater position than, in a ranking.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, John 1:15:
quote.text: He that cometh after me is preferred before me.

quote.text: All this was extraordinarily distasteful to Churchill. It was ugly, gross. Never before had he felt such repulsion when the vicar displayed his characteristic bluntness or coarseness of speech. In the present connexion—or rather as a transition from the subject that started their conversation—such talk had been distressingly out of place.

definitions.definition: (chiefly literary or poetic) In advance in position or sequence; ahead.

quote.citation: 1896, Hilaire Belloc, “The Elephant”, in The Bad Child’s Book of Beasts:
quote.text: When people call this beast to mind,They marvel more and moreAt such a little tail behind,So LARGE a trunk before.

definitions.definition: In advance of the time when.
